title: JPM, GS, MS Stocks Edge Higher After-Hours — Banks Lift Dividends And Announce Buybacks After Fed Stress Test - Stocktwits
content: Shares of JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM), Morgan Stanley (MS) and Goldman Sachs (GS) edged higher in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the banks announced higher dividends and buybacks following the Federal Reserve’s stress test, which showed the banking sector remains well positioned to withstand a severe economic downturn. At the time of writing, JPM stock was up 0.6% after-hours after closing the regular session down 0.21%, while MS shares gained 0.4% and GS stock was up 0.1%. JPMorgan Chase & Co announced a $50-billion share repurchase program and raised its quarterly dividend as part of updated shareholder return plans. The bank said its board also intends to increase its quarterly dividend 10% to $1.65 per share, up from $1.50 per share, for the third quarter of 2026. The new buyback program will take effect from July 1, alongside the updated shareholder return plans. Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase, said, “The Board’s intended dividend increase is supported by our consistent investment in our business and strong financial performance. The new share repurchase program provides us with the flexibility to deploy capital in ways that enhance shareholder value over time.” Goldman Sachs (GS) also increased its quarterly dividend by 11% to $5 per share from $4.50, pointing to strong earnings momentum and a robust capital position. The revised payout implies an annual dividend of $20 and will take effect on July 1, pending board approval. Morgan Stanley (MS) similarly announced a 15% hike in its quarterly dividend to $1.15 per share from $1. In addition, the firm said its board has reauthorized a multi-year share repurchase program of up to $20 billion, with no fixed end date, set to begin in the third quarter. The announcement by JPMorgan Chase & Co comes after the U.S. Federal Reserve released the results of its annual stress test. It showed that large banks are well positioned to withstand a severe recession and continue lending to households and businesses. The Fed said that despite more than $708 billion in total loan losses under the hypothetical scenario, aggregate capital declined only 1.6 percentage points and remained above minimum requirements. It added that all 32 banks tested stayed above their minimum common equity tier 1 capital requirements under a scenario that included a severe global recession, a 39% drop in commercial real estate prices, a 30% fall in house prices and an unemployment rate peaking at 10%. Retail sentiment for MS turned ‘bearish’ amid ‘high’ message volume, while GS’ sentiment remained ‘neutral’ with ‘normal’ activity levels. Year-to-date, JPM stock is up around 0.4% and MS shares have gained about 21%. The GS stock, meanwhile, has lost around 1.5% in the same period. (QCOM) jumped nearly 15% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the company outlined a series of updated fiscal 2029 revenue targets at its investor day. Apart from the revenue targets, Qualcomm also announced a deal with Meta Platforms (META) to use its chips in AI-focused data center infrastructure. Earlier, during the regular trading session on Wednesday, QCOM shares ended 3.29% lower. The chipmaker raised its non-handset revenue target to $40 billion, about double its previous fiscal 2029 target. It also announced a comprehensive data center AI infrastructure strategy with a revenue target of more than $15 billion a year by fiscal 2029. It also set targets of over $14 billion from IoT, $8 billion from industrial, networking and robotics, and $6 billion from personal AI and compute. Qualcomm said its automotive business is on track to exit FY2026 at a $6-billion annualized revenue run rate, while its automotive design-win pipeline has grown to $65 billion. It expects automotive revenue to reach $10 billion by fiscal 2029. The company added that handsets will account for about one-third of QCT revenue by fiscal 2029, within a projected $1.7 trillion total addressable market by 2030. Qualcomm announced a deal with Meta Platforms (META) under which Qualcomm will supply data center CPUs for Meta’s infrastructure, including its Dragonfly C1000 chip. The processor is expected to power Meta’s next-generation server fleet and support future data center expansion, with production set to begin in the second half of 2028. Qualcomm said the Dragonfly C1000 is a data center CPU designed for agentic AI workloads, aimed at delivering strong computing performance while keeping power consumption low. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company is “excited to continue partnering with Qualcomm Technologies” as it builds next-generation CPUs to support its AI ambitions. Zuckerberg added that Meta is working toward delivering “personal superintelligence to everyone in the world.” Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said the partnership reflects an expansion “from devices to data center,” calling it “just the beginning.” Qualcomm said it has secured two major hyperscaler deals that are expected to generate meaningful revenue, while its custom silicon business is projected to begin contributing meaningful revenue from Q1 2027. The company also expanded its partnership with Hugging Face to support developer-driven AI across devices and cloud infrastructure. Separately, Qualcomm said earlier on Wednesday that it has agreed to acquire software infrastructure firm Modular in a $3.92-billion deal. The chipmaker said the acquisition is aimed at strengthening its ability to deliver a more optimized artificial intelligence compute layer. SpaceX shares rose 1% premarket on Wednesday, bucking concerns over rising short interest, lockup-related selling pressure, and a former SEC chair’s warning that IPO excitement could give way to a “great rebalancing.” SPCX stock fell as low as $147.11 early Tuesday, slipping below the $150 level from its first Nasdaq trading day after the June 11 IPO. The stock later recovered, ending Tuesday up about 1% at near $156. About 40 million SpaceX shares are currently sold short, representing roughly 5% to 7% of the company’s publicly tradable float of about 625 million shares, according to S3 Partners. Borrow conditions also do not point to the squeeze pressure. More than 30 million SpaceX shares are available to borrow, while annualized borrowing fees are below 1%, S3 said, according to CNBC. “SPCX has attracted active short-selling interest, but the data suggest this is far from a supply-constrained short,” said Matthew Unterman, head of research at S3. “The current setup looks more like normal price discovery than a classic short-squeeze candidate.” Coatue investor said in a CNBC interview that the firm is not rushing to cash out. When asked whether Coatue would keep or sell its SpaceX shares, he said, “I’m going to keep them,” noting that the shares must be held for six months after receipt. After the lockup, he said the decision becomes “more of a portfolio decision,” based on how large SpaceX becomes relative to the rest of the firm’s holdings. “We own a significant amount of SpaceX,” he said, while adding that some of his biggest mistakes came from “optimizing for the short run.” He pointed to Nvidia as a lesson, calling his decision to sell “one of the bigger mistakes” he had made. “Sometimes you’re like, ‘Oh, maybe I’m so clever. I can sell out of this and buy that.’ It rarely works,” he said. Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler offered a more cautious view, saying that the wave of mega IPOs, including SpaceX, could be a “tell” about where the market cycle stands. He said that markets are funding a major AI infrastructure boom, but warned that some valuations are running at “100, 140 times revenues without earnings,” according to Bloomberg. Gensler said it is possible that the market looks back in six months and finds the IPO wave was “fine.” However, he also warned there is an “equal and better chance” that venture capitalists and sovereign wealth funds begin selling as lockups expire. “I call it the great rebalancing,” Gensler said. “All those venture capitalists and sovereign wealth funds, they’re going to want to take risk off the page.” He said tha investors could move to reduce “a third, a half, maybe three quarters” of their exposure, creating “a lot of selling pressure” as shares become available. Shares of The Wendy’s Company surged more than 20% in overnight trading after a combination of executive leadership changes and intense retail investor activity thrust the restaurant chain into the spotlight. If the gains hold through Wednesday’s session, the stock would be on track for its strongest single-day advance in more than five years. Investor enthusiasm picked up after Wendy’s named two former Potbelly Sandwich executives as its new chief financial officer and chief executive officer, as the beleaguered fast-food chain attempts a hard turnaround. The news quickly became a focal point for traders seeking signs of a broader recovery story. At the same time, online trading communities identified Wendy’s as a potential short-squeeze candidate. The stock climbed to the top of the trending list on Stocktwits and became one of the most talked-about names on Reddit’s WallStreetBets forum. Traders highlighted the company’s profitability, relatively low valuation and sizable dividend yield as reasons the stock differs from some speculative meme-stock names that dominated headlines during the 2021 trading frenzy. Some even argued that a large bearish position in the stock created conditions that could force short sellers to repurchase shares if prices continued rising. Short interest in the stock is at a record level of 26.4%, according to Koyfin data. Such positioning can amplify gains when investors betting against a company rush to close their trades. The stock’s move higher appeared to trigger exactly that dynamic, with buying activity intensifying ahead of Wednesday’s session. The sudden optimism follows a challenging period for the restaurant operator. Wendy’s stock lost nearly 40% over the past year and touched a twenty-year low on Tuesday as consumers cut discretionary spending amid high inflation and fast-food chains competed aggressively on pricing. Wendy’s reported a 5.5% drop in global sales during the first quarter, largely because sales at its existing U.S. restaurants weakened. Profit margins were also squeezed by lower customer traffic and higher food expenses. U.S. same-store sales fell 7.8% in the quarter, worsening from a 2.8% decline a year earlier. title: A Valles Caldera ride proves better with company - Albuquerque Journal
content: Support local news. Please select your privacy preferences to continue. A New Mexico adventure motorcyclist joins GS Riders of New Mexico for a scenic group ride I stumbled upon a paradox when I first got into adventure motorcycle riding. I was drawn to the allure of setting out on the open road, just me and my bike, to explore the byways and dirt roads that crisscross vast swaths of our beautiful country. I soon discovered that for reasons of safety and enjoyment, however, this is a hobby best shared with other riders. I bought my 2012 Yamaha Super Tenere — a 1,200 c.c. motorcycle suspended in such a way as to make long stretches of highway and bumpy dirt roads equally manageable — back in spring of 2020. Originally, I was fixated on a BMW model of similar capabilities but for a much higher price tag. I had even sent a few thousand dollars of earnest money to the friend from whom I was to purchase the Beemer when a small hiccup bubbled up. A pandemic, to be precise. My friend kindly refunded me the money. In that moment none of us was very confident of what our financial futures would look like. I cut my budget in half and went shopping for something more affordable. Some people took solace in a new pet to cope with COVID, others binge-watched television or took up cooking. I rode a motorcycle. Six years later, I’m still deeply in love with this big blue bike. I was living in Vermont when I acquired my COVID cure but returned to New Mexico in 2023 after an eight-year absence. Here my network of riding buddies is much smaller. Without a group to ride with on the regular, my motorcycle has spent too much time collecting dust in my already overstuffed one-car garage. Skewing shy by nature, I’ve struggled to make friends with similar interests, infrastructure and calendars. So, on a recent weekend I did something I thought I’d never do; I met up with a Facebook group for a planned ride. I’ve been lurking on GS Riders of New Mexico for more than a year now, always finding excuses not to show up and ride along. But when member Gary Talda announced he’d be leading a ride into the Valles Caldera backcountry, I couldn’t find a reason not to go. On a chilly October Saturday morning I made my way to the designated meeting point — the Home Depot parking lot on U.S. Route 550 in Rio Rancho — rolling gracefully up to the line of motorcycles already assembled. I promptly stalled my bike to a lurching halt. On the bright side, I remembered to put my kickstand down before I dismounted. I walked up to the group of six other riders and introduced myself. I was immediately aware that in almost every case, we all were meeting each other for the first time. Talda had us circle up for a quick briefing. He reviewed the route we’d be taking — U.S. Route 550 to N.M. State Road 4 (NM 4) all the way to the entrance of the Valles Caldera National Preserve. Talda warned us that he’d be setting his cruise control at the speed limit, and if anyone was feeling spicy, they should not hesitate to pass him; we would all meet at the visitor center at Valles Caldera. Otherwise, we were advised to ride in a staggered formation and maintain a safe distance between bikes. Tom Peterson, an active member of GS Riders of NM and a very experienced rider, would tail behind as the “sweeper” to make sure none of us lambs went astray. It’s typical to have the strongest rider in a group play this role. I was second to last in the chain. I chose not to read into that. It was a spectacular October morning with cloudless, deep blue skies and temperatures hovering in the upper 50s as we rolled north. I realized quickly that I was a little under layered for the weather, but the sunshine and my heated grips were enough to stave off hypothermia. Riding or even driving up N.M. 4 is usually a treat, and today was no exception. The wide canyon from San Ysidro gradually narrows as the road winds and climbs along the Jemez River through Jemez Pueblo and Jemez Springs, with deep red rocks all around and soaring canyon walls framing the valley. The previous week’s heavy rain had left dried red mud across many stretches of the road, and I spotted an occasional boulder that had come to rest on the shoulder, suggesting the rains had been significant. But there were no road hazards of note. When our group reached the north end of Jemez Springs, we were stuck behind a volunteer police officer who kept us honest all the way to the intersection of N.M. 4 and New Mexico Road 126 (N.M. 126) in La Cueva. Given the fairly heavy traffic and brisk air temperatures, I was happy to not be racing around the tight corners. The slower pace allowed more time and attention span to take in the scenery and kept the wind chill at bay. We reached the Valles Caldera National Preserve Visitor Center around 10:30 a.m. The sun had marched higher in the sky, but its warming effects were mitigated by our much higher altitude. The digital thermometer on my instrument cluster told me it was 57 degrees, but often it reads higher because of the waste heat from the engine. It felt closer to 50 to me. Two riders, Levi from Carlsbad and Damond from Bosque Farms, were waiting for us as we pulled into the heavily graveled parking area, where my front wheel washed out and I very nearly dropped my 585-pound machine. That would prove to be the most technically challenging terrain of the entire ride. We were now nine motorcycles strong as we marched into the visitor center and descended on the park ranger, who quickly organized us. Half of our number sported annual America the Beautiful passes that admitted two people, meaning the other half of us were able to piggyback for free and avoid the $20 daily admission fee. All of us had secured a $2 backcountry permit online prior to the ride (only 40 per day are issued, so it’s best to reserve in advance at Recreation.gov), and once we proved this, the ranger gave us each a numeric code that would allow us to open the gate into the backcountry. A quick potty break and then we all mounted up and made our way to the backcountry entrance. Rolling through the gate, I realized that this was as deep into the Valles Caldera as I had ever ventured despite many visits to the preserve over the years. My expectations were high, and I was not disappointed. We followed the well-maintained gravel road for about 10 miles, surrounded by the vast, grassy meadows of the caldera interrupted here and there by forested bluffs. An occasional pothole, a couple of mud puddles, and stretches of mild washboard surfaces were all the obstacles we encountered. I’d have been very comfortable driving a standard passenger car on this road in these conditions. While the riding itself was tame, the scenery was enough to get my adrenaline flowing. I knew in my head that the caldera was some 14 miles across and almost 90,000 acres, but the scale can’t be captured by the numbers. Only by traversing this expanse did I fully appreciate just how massive an eruption it must have been to create it 1.2 million years ago. We came to a T-intersection and turned right — almost due east — following this leg about eight miles to its end near the headwaters of San Antonio Creek, which flows west to join the Jemez River before making its way to the Rio Grande. We passed a large group of folks sporting fly fishing rods who appeared to be part of a clinic. Though the creek is narrow enough to jump across in most places, it is home to a healthy population of brown trout and is a popular destination for anglers willing to make the trek. We turned around and backtracked to the T-intersection, then proceeded west for a few miles to the road’s terminus. Here we dismounted and ate what provisions we had brought. We milled about for a bit, chatting and getting to know one another a little better. Most of us were of the gray-haired variety, but there were younger, fitter riders represented as well. Except for Levi, who had ridden up from his home in Carlsbad a few days earlier to camp and explore the general area, all of us called the Albuquerque Metropolitan Area home. This happened to be the opening day of the Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta, an event we all support but which also makes motorcyclists more than a little uncomfortable. Even without balloon-bewildered drivers, a motorcycle frequently goes unnoticed on the highway, too often with tragic results. In an average year, about 50 riders are killed in New Mexico, and about twice that number are seriously injured. Distracted driving surely is a factor in many cases, as are alcohol and unsafe riding practices. I simply refuse to ride into Albuquerque during Balloon Fiesta, and for the rest of the year I avoid riding in town as much as possible. Today’s ride was as safe as they come thanks to the remote location, perfect weather, and the fact that all of our group were equipped with full safety gear and competent riding skills. Talda called us back into a circle as we prepared to depart. He invited us to follow him as he backtracked our route via N.M. 4 and U.S. 550. Alternatively, Peterson would lead a group on a more circuitous route up N.M. 126, then south on the unpaved Forest Service Road 376 to Gilman Tunnels before reconnecting with N.M. 4 near Jemez Pueblo. A third group would venture south on Forrest Service Road 10 into Ponderosa, also rejoining N.M. 4 near Jemez Pueblo. Having ridden both routes before and feeling a bit stiff in my aging lower back from the 100 or so miles I’d already logged today, I opted to stay on the paved roads. I stopped at a gas station near the Walatowa Visitor Center to top off my now half-empty gas tank. I winced at the price of just three gallons of premium fuel. In sixth gear cruising down the highway, I can nurse about 50 miles per gallon, but on the twisty, hilly roads of the Jemez Mountains and high-revving backcountry route through the preserve, I guessed I was averaging closer to 25 miles per gallon. I’m a cheap man by nature; this fool and his money do not like to part ways. But while my fuel efficiency may have taken a hit on this ride, the smiles per gallon came at a nominal cost. If you’re riding a motorcycle in the Jemez Mountains in October with a good bunch of people, you are likely having a good day. I’m resolved to be a regular tag-along with the GS Riders of New Mexico. title: What To Expect In Markets This Week: JPM, GS, C Bank Earnings, CPI Report, Kevin Warsh's Speech And More - Stocktwits
content: Wall Street is heading into a busy week with investors watching a fresh batch of corporate results and several key economic developments that could shape the market's direction. The week will bring earnings from some of the biggest names in the financial sector, along with new inflation data and a closely watched speech from Federal Reserve Governor Kevin Warsh. The banking sector will take center stage this week as JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM), Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS) and Citigroup Inc. (C) report quarterly results, giving investors an early look at how Wall Street's biggest financial institutions are navigating the current market environment. Carr said the FCC’s approach is focused on getting more spectrum into the hands of companies willing to invest and compete, rather than deciding which technologies or providers will ultimately win. “We're seeing a lot of competition. We're seeing a lot of innovation,” Carr said. He pointed to the FCC’s plans to bring more than $100 billion worth of spectrum into the market over the next two years, arguing that increased competition should ultimately benefit consumers. Carr expects the resulting competition to translate into faster service and lower prices, describing the current environment as “really interesting.” He also suggested that the wireless market is entering a period where traditional carriers, satellite operators and technology companies could increasingly compete on the same playing field. A key piece of SpaceX’s strategy is the spectrum it has accumulated as it pushes Starlink toward a broader mobile offering. Carr noted that SpaceX already obtained mid-band spectrum through its deal involving EchoStar and now has access to low-band spectrum as well. That combination could become particularly important because different portions of the wireless spectrum serve different purposes. Low-band spectrum travels farther and penetrates buildings more effectively, while higher bands can deliver greater capacity but have shorter range. Mid-band sits between the two, offering what Carr called the “Goldilocks” combination. “People are serious about getting into the terrestrial game. You're going to want a portfolio that includes both mid-band and low band,” he added. Carr said FCC is also moving to make additional spectrum available for direct-to-device services, which allow smartphones to connect directly to satellites. The biggest uncertainty is whether SpaceX intends to become a conventional wireless carrier rather than simply using satellites to supplement existing networks to compete with AT&T Inc. Carr said the FCC will not pick the winner. “We're going to step back and watch it,” he said. Americans are more worried about their finances than at any point in the University of Michigan’s 75-year consumer survey, according to economist Peter Schiff, who says the data directly contradicts President Donald Trump’s claims that the U.S. economy is the strongest in history. Schiff pointed to the latest consumer sentiment data, which showed sentiment falling to 46.3 in October from 48.1 in September, while one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7%, from 4.6% in September. The biggest warning, according to Schiff, came from the survey’s current conditions index, which hit a record low. “Not once during these 75 years were Americans as worried about their personal finances as they are right now,” Schiff said. That period includes the Korean War, the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Vietnam War, the 1970s oil crisis, the Gulf War, 9/11, the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. “Yet throughout all of that, all that bad stuff, the consumer wasn't as worried as he is today,” he said. Schiff argued that the data is particularly difficult to reconcile with Trump’s repeated claims that the economy is booming. “Donald Trump says the economy has never been better in history. So apparently, even though we have the greatest economy we've ever had, consumers are more worried about their own personal economic circumstances than they've ever been,” he added. “The idea that we have a great economy is pure fiction.” Schiff also argued that voters are increasingly blaming the Trump administration for economic conditions rather than continuing to blame former President Joe Biden. Schiff said the strength of financial markets is masking the pressure being felt by households without substantial investments. He pointed to rising loan delinquencies and debt-to-income ratios as signs that consumers are struggling despite the strong stock market. “If times were good, people's incomes would be rising. Their debt would be falling relative to those rising incomes,” Schiff said. “But the fact that the debts are rising, it's because incomes are not rising. Families are struggling.” At the same time, Schiff noted that older Americans have benefited significantly from rising asset prices. “Why are these retirees that don't even have jobs? Why are they getting so rich? Because they own stocks,” he said. Schiff argued that the same monetary policies that have pushed asset prices higher have also contributed to rising living costs. “Yes, Trump is right about that. We got a bull market. We have record high stock prices. But it's the same bad monetary and economic policies that are driving the cost of living up and that are undermining the economy that are also responsible for inflated asset prices,” he added. Schiff's biggest concern is what happens when elevated interest rates collide with America’s enormous debt burden. He argued that investors have become conditioned to believe that the ultra-low rates seen after the 2008 financial crisis were normal. “People are delusional when they think that what we're seeing now is the aberration. No, we've been living in the aberration,” Schiff said. He believes the economy is now moving back toward historically higher rates, which creates a serious problem for the U.S., he argued, because government debt is far higher than it was during previous periods of elevated rates. “We are in a position where we have high debt and high interest rates. In fact, we have higher debt than we've ever had and we may end up with higher interest rates than we've ever had,” Schiff explained. Schiff therefore expects Treasury yields to remain under pressure even as many investors continue to bet that rates will eventually fall back toward the levels seen over the past decade. “We are normalizing right now with rates going up,” Schiff said. (QCOM) CEO Cristiano Amon says the smartphone is about to become a much more powerful AI machine, with some leading AI companies already asking the chip maker to ensure future phones can run models with as many as 100 billion parameters. During a recent episode of the Sources podcast, Amon said the shift could set the stage for a new battle among AI agents, with smartphones playing a critical role in deciding which assistants ultimately win. Qualcomm shares declined about 0.3% during the regular trading session on Friday, and edged lower by another 0.1% in the after-hours trade. The AI industry is already looking beyond today’s chatbot-style smartphone experiences, according to Amon. The Qualcomm CEO said some companies at the forefront of AI are asking Qualcomm to prepare for a future where extremely large models can run directly on smartphones. “Some AI companies right now, some of the companies at the forefront of AI are telling Qualcomm, by 2028 I need to make sure that I have the ability to run at least a 100 billion parameter model into a phone,” Amon said. He added that those companies want the models to be capable of running continuously on the device. While many of today's AI agents rely heavily on cloud computing, Amon believes increasingly capable phones will handle a growing share of the work locally. The reason, he argued, is that the phone contains information that is uniquely tied to its owner. That includes personal context, app data and sensor information that can make AI agents more useful and potentially more private when processing happens on-device. Amon sees the AI smartphone as something considerably different from simply putting a chatbot on a handset. Instead, he expects AI agents to interact with the apps, data and services already living on the device and take actions on a user's behalf. “There’s going to be a battle of the agents,” Amon said. Compared to the AI feature on smartphones today, which largely resemble standalone tools, Amon envisions something more deeply integrated into the operating system and applications. “You're just going to say, you get a question, you're going to say, ‘Yes,’ and then the agent is going to do things for you,” he said. Amon argues that the cloud and the device won't necessarily compete for AI workloads. He sees the two as an integrated computing system, with the phone acting as a highly personalized endpoint for AI. “If you pull up your phone and it takes time for the agent to do certain things for you, then you're going to do it yourself. But certain things you're going to just get the agent to do it,” he said. Amon's AI smartphone thesis comes as the broader smartphone market faces a difficult period, with memory costs putting additional pressure on device prices. But he argues the weakness is not necessarily a sign that consumers have lost interest in smartphones. Instead, the market has matured into a replacement-driven business, while the premium segment continues to expand. “The premium and the high tier as a percentage of the total market continue to expand,” Amon said. He believes AI could provide the next major reason for consumers to upgrade. “Once you put the harness in, you put the capability, you will see how those things are going to develop. And I think that's going to change the phone experience,” he said. Amon believes it could make smartphones an important part of the AI compute landscape even as the company expands into data centers, PCs, cars and wearables. “Phones are not going to go anywhere. It is the largest development platform ever created by mankind,” he said. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around Qualcomm trended in the ‘bearish’ territory at the time of writing. BMW has released new details for the 2027 F 450 GS, adding fresh technical information and finalizing trim‑level equipment for the U.S. market. Last year, we announced the global reveal of BMW’s new lightweight parallel‑twin platform — a major step forward from the outgoing G 310 GS — and the core specifications remain unchanged. What BMW provides now is a deeper look at the engineering behind the chassis, controls, and exhaust system, along with clearer confirmation of how the bike will be packaged for U.S. buyers. With the F 450 GS positioned as BMW’s new entry point into the GS lineup, riders have been eager to see how the compact twin stacks up in an increasingly competitive segment. The latest release fills in several gaps from the original announcement but before diving into those updates, it’s worth revisiting what this new small‑displacement adventure bike brings to the category. The F 450 GS is powered by a 420cc liquid‑cooled parallel twin producing 48 hp at 8,750 rpm and 32 lb‑ft of torque at 6,750 rpm. BMW designed the compact twin around a 135‑degree crankshaft to enhance traction feel and deliver a more characterful exhaust note, pairing it with a 13.0:1 compression ratio and electronic fuel injection. Power runs through a 6‑speed transmission, and riders choosing the Sport or GS Trophy trims also receive Gear Shift Assist Pro for clutchless upshifts and downshifts. BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch (ERC), standard on the GS Trophy and optional elsewhere, automatically modulates clutch engagement to prevent stalling while preserving full engine braking, yet can be overridden manually when the rider wants full control. From there, the bike’s chassis builds on a tubular steel frame with the engine acting as a stressed member to increase rigidity and reduce overall weight. The Sport Suspension on the GS Trophy model is handled by a KYB 43mm rebound- and compression-adjustable USD fork offering 7.1 inches of travel, working in tandem with a KYB WAD rear shock that provides spring preload and rebound adjustment along with travel‑dependent damping. A hollow‑cast aluminum swingarm helps reduce unsprung weight, and tubeless cross‑spoked wheels come standard on the GS Trophy variant. Ergonomics follow a neutral riding triangle designed for both seated and standing control, supported by seat height options of 32.7, 33.3, and 34.0 inches. BMW includes adjustable brake and clutch levers, as well as adjustable gearshift and footbrake levers, giving riders more flexibility to tailor the cockpit for off‑road use. Rounding out the package is a full suite of electronics that includes Rain, Road, and Enduro riding modes, with Enduro Pro reserved for the Sport and GS Trophy. ABS Pro, Dynamic Traction Control (DTC), Engine Drag Torque Control (MSR), and Dynamic Brake Control (DBC) provide additional support, while a 6.5‑inch TFT display with smartphone connectivity comes standard along with full LED lighting and a USB‑C charging port. BMW claims a top speed of 102 mph and 0–62 mph in 5.9 seconds, giving the F 450 GS respectable highway performance for a small‑bore adventure bike while still maintaining the compact footprint needed for off‑road maneuverability. BMW’s latest announcement provides a clearer picture of the bike’s component design and adjustability. The Bavarian manufacturer now specifies that the new alloy wheels on the base model are 2.2 lbs lighter than those on the G 310 GS, reducing unsprung weight and improving responsiveness. They also confirm that both the gearshift and footbrake levers are adjustable, along with the brake and clutch hand levers, giving riders more flexibility in tailoring the cockpit for off‑road use. Additional clarity was provided on the exhaust system, which uses a stainless‑steel design with two catalytic converters, and on the rear suspension, which employs a KYB central spring strut with preload and rebound adjustment and travel‑dependent damping (WAD). BMW also notes that the hollow‑cast aluminum swingarm contributes to both weight savings and rigidity. Cross‑spoked wheels, standard on the GS Trophy, will be available as an option on other trims beginning with July 2027 production. Finally, BMW has provided a more detailed explanation of how their Easy Ride Clutch system works. Previously described only as an anti‑stall feature, they now explain that the system automatically adds a small amount of clutch slip whenever engine speed drops too low, helping prevent stalls during slow, technical maneuvers or abrupt downshifts. At the same time, it keeps enough mechanical connection to maintain a natural engine‑braking feel, rather than disengaging the clutch completely. BMW also clarified that ERC is fully overrideable: the moment the rider uses the clutch lever deliberately, the system steps aside. BMW states the F 450 GS will reach U.S. dealers in Q1 2027, finalizing the rollout window previously estimated between late 2026 and early 2027. title: A Little Hell-Raiser: We Drive the 1992 Mazda MX-3 GS - Car and Driver
content: A car that winks at you. And then sings and dances too. “Mazda will make vehicles that wink at you,” proclaimed chairman Kenichi Yamamoto. As mission statements go, that’s a catchy line. The MX-3 has an air about it. Sitting there, looking quirky and racy and maybe even a little frivolous, it kind of grins a conspiratorial grin. It chucks you under the chin with a promise of fun times to come. “Hey, you’re not doing anything. Whaddya say we go raise a little hell?” A car that winks at you? When it appears this fall, the MX-3 will run in the small sports-specialty category, a class bursting at its little seams with such sporty coupes as the new Toyota Pa­seo and Nissan NX, plus the familiar Isuzu Impulse/Geo Storm and Honda CRX. (The CRX is the lone two-plus­-none among a pack of two-plus-twos.) Mazda hopes, however, that you’ll view the MX-3 a little differently. Not so much as another zippy two-plus-two coupe based on cheap-sedan hardware, but rath­er as a sports car with distinction. Two distinctions, actually: real four-passenger capacity, and the automotive world’s smallest V-6 engine. See all results for used 1992 Mazda MX-3 for sale near 50317 We wonder just how “real” that occu­pancy rate is, but there’s no denying that this high-revving, four-cam 1845 cc six in­troduces a new class of powerplant, bring­ing to the small-coupe segment the silky snarl that comes only from sixes. (Mazda is also looking to steal thunder from Volkswagen, which after many years of struggle is just now readying its narrow-­angle V-6 for production in the Corrado.) Catchy styling makes the right first im­pression, combining rounded forms, a wedgy profile, a sharply raked windshield (65 degrees from vertical), and a vast, wrap-over rear window. It looks sharp, and heads swivel all around the MX-3 on the road. Aero add-ons help trim the Cd to 0.31. Notable aesthetic details include the curvature at the rear edge of the side win­dows and a tiny glass panel beneath the rear spoiler, in the batch’s vertical face. The latter is touted as an aid to visibility but seems so shallow as to be more useful as a styling element, to keep the tail from looking too thick and flat. Wheelbase (96.3 inches) and front and rear track (57.5 and 57.7 inches) are very generous for this class, giving the MX-3 a big footprint—which is a promising start for good handling—as well as a surpris­ingly roomy cabin. From the driver’s po­sition, the interior looks wide, open, and spacious. It also looks attractive and well laid out, though much less distinctively contoured than the sheetmetal. The front seats easily accommodate large adults without crowding, and they offer good side bolstering that stops short of impeding entry and exit. And what of that back seat, which Mazda claims is not a “plus-two” penalty box, but a place where average-size people can ride “in reasonable posture”? It is quite wide (and attractive, with a continuous, wrap­around effect at back and sides but clearly defined bun pockets), but an occupant’s head, knees, and feet need to be located precisely where Mazda intended in order to find a fit. It is possible to carry two adults back there, but they should be good sports—literally, because it’s an athletic clamber into place—and the trip shouldn’t be much farther than down to the video store. See all results for used 1992 Mazda MX-3 for sale near 50317 Most of the car’s sloping front end is over the horizon from the driver’s eye, a minor packaging miracle considering the giant lump of engine the hood has to cov­er. Though 1.8 liters is hardly a lot of swept volume, it takes a load of far-flung aluminum to enclose it and its valve gear and manifolding in a V configuration. One glance at the outbreak of cam covers and intake runners under the MX-3’s hood shows why orthodoxy for these effi­ciency-minded coupes is four cylinders in a neat little row. But it all fits, and an impressive collec­tion of machinery it is. The transversely mounted V-6’s main castings are all-alu­minum, with the cylinder banks angled at 60 degrees. Twin camshafts in each cylinder head operate four valves per cylinder, whose breathing efficiency is aided by an intake tract that uses two solenoid-controlled butterfly valves to vary its effective volume and fatten the torque curve. Mazda engineers correctly anticipated that low- and mid-range torque was going to need help in this short-stroke, high-­rpm engine, and some drivers are sure to wonder if it got enough. The SAE net out­put ratings are 130 horsepower at 6500 rpm and 115 pound-feet of torque at 4500 (numbers that meet or beat those of every car in the class except the NX2000’s 140 hp and 130 pound-feet). But on the go, the free-spinning little six often seems to gen­erate the sensations of speed more effec­tively than it does real thrust. Around 3000 rpm, the exhaust reso­nates with a gorgeous snarl that evokes the E-type Jaguar 3.8, yet there’s little power to be had down there. Not until 4500 does the small of your back start to register acceleration, and then only in the lower gears. Rapid progress demands lots of revs, like in the range from 5000 to the 7000-rpm redline. That can feel a trifle overdramatic in traffic, but at least the en­gine is happy to do it. It’s marvelously smooth and responsive, though up there, the Jaguar snarl is replaced by a muted whir that recalls Mazda’s rotary engine. A light-action, rod-linkage gearbox provides smooth if slightly long throws for stirring through the five ratios. The five-speed’s gear spacing is probably as good as it can be, but the one-two gap is pretty broad. Peg the tach in first (33 mph at 7000 rpm) and the shift to second drops revs all the way to about 3900—a bit be­low the fringe of torque territory. As soon as we can mate a production MX-3 to our instruments, we—and you—will know a lot more about how the impressions from this pre-production example translate into hard performance data. Fortunately, a well-sorted chassis con­tributes to the MX-3’s back-road fun fac­tor. And, for that matter, to its freeway composure. This is the company, remem­ber, that coined the term “stagility,” de­noting a combination of stability and agil­ity. And the firm strut-type suspension, a refinement of the system used by the Pro­tege and Escort/Tracer sedans, does in fact give fine directional stability along with quick cornering response. Engine­-speed-sensitive power steering feels light and quick, and the dartiness we’ve no­ticed before in this rear-suspension design is much better controlled. There will actually be two MX-3s. The one we’ve been talking about is tagged the GS. There’s also a base model, but its 88-horsepower, SOHC 1.6-liter four, leaves it out of the real news. Differences include a disc/drum brake arrangement in place of the GS’s four-wheel discs, smaller tires (185/65 versus 205/55) on fourteen-inch steel wheels rather than the fifteen-inch alloys fitted to the GS, and a slower steer­ing ratio (17:1 compared with 15:1). An electronically controlled four-speed auto­matic can replace the manual box in ei­ther model, though we can’t imagine who would opt for it, especially with the playful, torqueless six. Prices have not yet been announced, but they will have to be competitive among small sporty coupes, meaning suggested retails in the low teens. The smooth and slinky MX-3 will shortly take its place among the RX-7, the Miata, and the MPV as the sort of specialized, off-center vehicle on which Mazda is building a name. If Mr. Yamamoto has his way, it will not only wink at you, but will also grab your sleeve and drag you off, promising an experience just a little different from what you’ve had with ev­erything else out there. 1992 Mazda MX-3 GSVehicle Type: front-engine, front-wheel-drive, 2+2-passenger, 2-door coupe ENGINEDOHC 24-valve V-6, aluminum block and heads, port fuel injectionDisplacement: 113 in3, 1845 cm3Power: 130 bhp @ 6500 rpmTorque: 115 lb-ft @ 4500 rpm CHASSISSuspension, F/R: struts/multilinkBrakes, F/R: 10.1-in vented disc/9.8-in discTire Size: P205/55VR-15 DIMENSIONSWheelbase: 96.3 inLength: 165.7 inWidth: 66.7 inHeight: 51.6 inPassenger Volume, F/R: 49/30 ft3Cargo Volume: 15 ft3Curb Weight: 2550 lb C/D PERFORMANCE ESTIMATES60 mph: 8.5 sec1/4-Mile: 16.0 sec @ 85 mphTop Speed: 125 mph Front-Wheel-Drive Heresy? title: Competition Among China’s AI Models Is Intensifying as the Chip Sector Advances - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The competition between makers of China’s artificial intelligence (AI) models is intensifying, raising questions among investors on the sustainability of leadership in model performance, with increasing focus on cost efficiencies and the harness layer.  At the same time, the country’s capacity for building semiconductors is showing signs of exceeding investor expectations, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Those insights were among the discussions at the second annual Goldman Sachs Asia Leaders Conference in Hong Kong, the firm’s largest client gathering in the region. The event featured companies that form the entire AI supply chain: 400 companies were represented and over 1,400 investors attended the event in Hong Kong. In many cases, the gap in performance, especially in coding, is narrowing between the leading AI models, says Ronald Keung, head of the Asia Internet Research team. “Intense competition on the model layer brings investor questions as to how AI-model developers can differentiate besides model performance,” Keung says. “The key may be in cost efficiencies and on the harness layer.” The harness layer refers to the ecosystem that houses and enables AI models. The harness allows the model to, among other things, access data and follow workflows. “The next key investments are focused more on the harness layer,” Keung says. “The AI labs in China actually are just beginning harness investments. In the past, the Chinese AI labs were more focused on the model layer.” Conference participants were also focused on China’s semiconductor sector, says Allen Chang, head of the Greater China Technology Research team. Officials in Beijing aim to increase the country’s self-sufficiency in AI and semiconductors. “There's always a lot of debate on China semiconductors,” Chang says. He says the development of China’s semiconductor industry—which includes chip design, tools for semiconductor manufacturing, silicon wafer fabrication, and the manufacturing of specialized AI chips—is progressing faster than he and the market expected. “The progress has surprised the market,” Chang says of China’s semiconductor industry. He points out that the local leading chip foundries in China have larger capacity expansion plans than analysts expected. At the same time, the semicap equipment makers (the tools for making semiconductor chips) have issued guidance for 40% year-on-year revenue increases over the next few years. Investors have noted that more of the makers of specialized computing chips for AI, the GPUs and ASICs, are listing shares on the public market, Chang says. “That’s why they need to announce their volumes in terms of production as well as technology migration,” he says. But even as the semiconductor industry advances, Chang says there are still bottlenecks—principally in the availability of GPUs. “Everything is driven by the GPU computing power.” And while there’s been progress, there are still constraints in terms of local foundry capacity and semicap equipment, he adds. Optical networking was another part of the AI ecosystem that was in focus at the conference, Chang says. Networking unlocks computing capability for AI chips and enables data exchange at low latencies. While copper cables and printed circuit boards are commonly used for short distance connections within servers, optical fiber connections have higher performance for long-distance or high-speed interconnections, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our analysts expect the total addressable market for this technology to increase by nine times to $154 billion in 2028. As the technology advances, investors may not fully appreciate the success that Chinese models have had in proliferating around the world, Keung says. While China’s AI technology faces geopolitical scrutiny in some jurisdictions, adoption is ongoing. He notes that Chinese open-weight large language models (LLMs) are being housed on US hyperscaler cloud systems, which could mark a step forward for these models reaching larger markets. By keeping their data and computing on domestic servers, countries with higher security thresholds could allow the use of Chinese AI models. “We're seeing that as an interesting development,” Keung says. In the meantime, China’s AI companies are taking different approaches to creating a competitive advantage, Keung says. Some are pushing for premium frontier status—to create the most advanced models—while others are attempting to be more cost efficient. “What the labs are trying to aim for is the best price-to-performance ratio,” he says. “Our view is the combination of these elements will lead to pricing power,” Keung says. “Cost efficiencies and the strongest financial power will lead to the most lasting success.” This document has been prepared by the Goldman Sachs Executive Office and is not a product of Goldman Sachs Global  Investment Research. title: Forget The Chevelle, This 2028 Buick Riviera Restomod Looks Absolutely Ruthless - HotCars
content: Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update A grille wide enough to intimidate a modern pickup truck, headlights that look ready to interrogate oncoming traffic, and a stance that would make speed bumps a proper concern.     Buick certainly knew how to make an entrance in the '60s, but this interpretation takes that attitude a touch further. This 1965 Buick Riviera GS restomod rendering reimagines one of Detroit's greatest luxury     Muscle Cars with modern performance styling, a brilliant stance, and enough visual appeal to embarrass some of the newer lot. When Buick introduced the Riviera in 1963, its objective was to challenge the     Ford Thunderbird's dominance of America's personal luxury car segment. Under the direction of legendary     General Motors designer Bill Mitchell, the Riviera adopted a dramatically different approach to American luxury. Its long hood, sweeping rear fenders, and clean bodywork gave it an almost European grand touring appearance. The design reached its peak in 1965, when Buick introduced vertically concealed headlights behind distinctive clamshell covers, creating one of the most recognizable front ends in Detroit's history. The real excitement arrived with the introduction of the 1965     Buick Riviera Gran Sport, or GS. Underneath its elegant bodywork sat a massive 425 Super Wildcat Nailhead V8 making 360 horsepower and 465 lb-ft of torque. Equipped with dual four-barrel carburetors, the engine was reportedly effortless and accompanied by the unmistakable soundtrack of American V8 muscle. That was serious firepower for a luxury coupe designed to transport its occupants in considerable comfort, especially when many performance cars were still struggling to combine refinement with outright speed. Buick also gave the Riviera GS mechanical upgrades worthy of its performance credentials. The Gran Sport package included a 3.42:1 Positraction rear axle, a freer-flowing dual exhaust system, and suspension improvements that sharpened handling. Power reached the rear wheels through a three-speed Super Turbine 400 automatic transmission featuring a variable-pitch torque converter. Despite weighing approximately 4,166 pounds, the Riviera GS could accelerate from 0-60 mph in around 7.2 seconds, impressive performance for a luxury coupe of its size and era. What made the 1965 Buick Riviera GS particularly interesting was its positioning within America's growing performance car landscape. The     Pontiac GTO and     Chevrolet Chevelle offered traditional muscle car excitement, while the Riviera went after people who wanted a powerful V8 wrapped in sophisticated styling. Its 117-inch wheelbase, distinctive bucket-seat interior, and relatively composed road manners made it a compelling American grand tourer. The rendering takes the Riviera's celebrated design and gives it the visual aggression of a much more modern muscle car. Up front, the famous vertical headlight arrangement remains recognizable, although modern LED lighting replaces the original concealed units. A substantial blacked-out grille dominates the nose, while a redesigned front bumper incorporates large lower air intakes and an aggressive splitter. The muscular front fenders retain their vintage character, creating an unusually convincing combination of '60s American luxury and plenty of modern touches. As for the profile, Buick's original long-hood, short-deck proportions remain beautifully preserved, but the restomod sits considerably closer to the pavement. Deep-dish alloy wheels fill the arches, accompanied by low-profile performance tires and a wider, more purposeful stance. The rich metallic burgundy paint changes character depending on the light, while the contrasting roof and carefully retained chrome trim maintain a connection to the original Riviera. At the back, horizontal LED taillights sit within a darkened rear panel, accompanied by prominent Buick lettering across the trunk lid. A redesigned rear bumper incorporates two large exhaust outlets, while the wide rear tires look pretty awesome and emphasize the car's personality. The original Riviera GS already had enough V8 torque to make its occupants appreciate the importance of comfortable seats. That said, a modern restomod project could take that performance considerably further. One possibility would involve retaining and upgrading the classic Nailhead V8, preserving the authentic character that makes the 1965 Buick Riviera GS special. Alternatively, a modern GM 6.2-liter V8 could provide the foundations for a considerably more powerful build, with 500 horsepower or more representing an achievable hypothetical target depending on the engine specification and modifications. Modernizing the drivetrain would also transform how this luxury muscle car behaves on American highways. A six-speed or 10-speed auto could improve acceleration, cruising refinement, and overall drivability compared with the original three-speed unit. Upgraded cooling, electronic fuel injection, and modern engine management would help support dependable performance. Given the Riviera's substantial weight and imposing dimensions, a properly engineered suspension setup and larger four-wheel disc brakes would be particularly important for those interested in enjoying their custom Buick beyond the occasional car show. Ultimately, this Buick Riviera GS restomod demonstrates how much untapped potential exists beyond America's usual muscle car favorites. Chevrolet Camaros, Pontiac GTOs, and classic Dodge Chargers have become familiar sights within the restomod world, but Buick's 1965 masterpiece is a relative virgin. Brilliant design, genuine V8 heritage, and luxury car sophistication means there's an excellent foundation for a sick custom build. If a talented American restomod specialist ever brings something resembling this rendering to life, Detroit's forgotten luxury muscle car could become one of the most desirable custom classics on the road. In The Markets podcast, he also discusses his outlook for mega-capitalization technology companies, stocks that benefit from German government spending, and US third-quarter earnings. Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Wednesday, October 7th, and I'm here in the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Mark Wilson, who is head of European Equities, Franchise Sales and Hedge Fund Coverage within our FICC and Equities Group. Mark, thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: Okay, Mark always great to have you here. Let's kick it off with the two headwinds in the market today. Rates have been going higher, oil's been going higher. Europe, of course, is exposed to both. What is Europe exposed to most, and what are clients caring about most here? Mark Wilson: In Europe, we are more vulnerable to the energy shock, and so the inflationary pressure is higher. If you think about the feed through to the markets, on six-month correlations, Euro stocks and 10-year Bund yields are about negative 70% correlated right now. You haven't seen that degree of negative correlation since back to the 1990s, so this is really a bit of a regime shift. You're right to ask the question though, because obviously over the last couple of weeks we've had a much more idiosyncratic event in Europe. OAT spreads versus Bunds have blown out, and some of the social, but mainly political issues focused around the upcoming budget in France have been a real problem. And so that's a major European specific issue, which is now there, and I think will be an ongoing feature over the next few months as we get towards the presidential elections in France in the first half of next year. Ultimately, here and now, the two things which clients are most focused on are the price behavior of that OAT-Bund spread, and also the energy and gas inventory stock situation as we head in towards winter. Chris Hussey: Okay, Mark, I get it. Oil more important than rates in Europe, but we also know that rates matter a lot to stocks. What are you seeing from clients around how rates are impacting stock valuation and positioning? Mark Wilson: In terms of equities specifically, and this isn't just common to Europe, you've seen a very logical de-rating in equity markets. So, S&P multiple has come down, same is true in Europe. If you look at the more rate sensitive parts of the market, if you look at European renewables, for example, they've de-rated at well over 20%, and so you've seen this quite logical re-rating, de-rating specifically, in equities in response to higher rates. You mentioned positioning. I think the most standout piece of information that we've been thinking about the last couple of weeks is just how much this has caused investors to reappraise their equity exposure and their equity risk. So, to put a number on this, we look at our fundamental hedge funds and their net exposure to the markets, and if you look at US-specific fundamental long-short clients today, their net length is in the north percentile on a one-year look-back. It's at a two and three percentile on a three-year and five-year look-back. I think globally, global fundamental long shorts, these are anywhere from nought to 9% in terms of their net length and exposure to the market. So positioning has been really cut in response to rates and a bunch of other uncertainties that are out there. Chris Hussey: Yeah. That, that is, that is a fascinating number, and nought, for our audience, is zero in England. So, let me expand, though, onto your energy comment, cause you make an interesting energy comment around how Europe is so exposed here. What many people don't realize is nat gas is the exposure as much as oil, and there have been, our commodities team has written about the potential for nat gas to really spike maybe five, ten times what you have to pay for nat gas in the US. Are you seeing that in the industrial complex of Europe yet? Are you seeing these in the numbers, or is this just something people are scared about and it's not something in the numbers yet? Mark Wilson: So it is in the numbers. Europe has definite competitive issues related to higher energy price costs, but this isn't new news. Europe trades cheaper. Part of it is this phenomena. These competitive threats are impacting industry and impacting the market. I do think, though, the starting point matters, and Europe is a lot cheaper than other global markets, especially the US, and so some of that is already in the price, and I don't think it's an impediment to performance. European banks have beaten Mag Seven on a one-year, three-year, four-year look-back, and so there's the opportunity for performance, but it's certainly a competitive headwind and issue for Europe. Chris Hussey: All right, Mark. 25 years ago, you were brokering me as a US analyst in Europe, so I know you know the US markets well. I know now -- Chris Hussey: Well, I know that you now know the European markets really well. So, I want you to compare US versus Europe here. Talk to me. Is Europe a value trap here with all the headwinds that they're facing, or is Europe an opportunity because it's so cheap? Mark Wilson: So part of the European discount is certainly because of the index composition. We have less tech, we have less high-growth companies, and so inevitably there is a value element to it. The European market has been holding its own. I mean, it's kept up with the US this year, and part of that is because there are some clear investment cycles within Europe, within industrials, within renewables, within defense. And what I'd say is the last few years have had a series of ongoing challenges to Europe, and Europe is slow to respond, but Europe is responding. So when you go back to COVID, there was a very large fiscal mobilization. Pretty soon afterwards, you had the Russia-Ukraine conflict and a real acknowledgment of a need for energy independence domestically. Not long after that, you had the challenge of the Iranian conflict and the obvious heightened energy issues, and the AI cycle in of itself is a challenge to Europe to respond, to have its own deployment. And so, within Europe, these forcing mechanisms have continued to compound and to drive action and to drive response. And so what I'd say is there are real themes to invest behind. That industrial theme, the rearmament of Europe, the drive for energy independence. And demographics has been one of the key issues for Europe and one of the key bear theses and one of the key planks of this value trap argument. This argument around demographics is destiny, I think, is somewhat being debunked when we think about the real power of AI and the deployment of AI, which will be very prevalent soon. Demographics times agents deployed in the economy could be a real uplift to demographically challenged areas. And so I think there's increasing hope that actually the European market offers real opportunity, and as the strategy to respond to these challenges becomes more evident. Chris Hussey: Okay. Third quarter earnings season is right upon us. We're going to kick it off in the United States tomorrow. Europe and the US, and the world more generally, is this peak earnings, or is this another opportunity to buy the earnings growth? Mark Wilson: So, I'm pretty sure in the US we have peak earnings growth for the third quarter. I think 27% earnings growth in the US, which is topping an amazing run in terms of earnings growth. And that's a clean earnings number, not taking benefit for all these one-time gains. Europe has actually been similarly strong, so we're forecasting 22% earnings growth year on year for the second half of this year. It's aided a little bit by the energy benefit, so there's a big composition within the index of energy companies. Clean of the energy stocks, we're still looking at 15% earnings growth. So yes, I think the second derivative is slowing, especially in the US, but the earnings growth environment speaks to that high nominal growth environment that we spoke about at the beginning. And given that we're now transitioning, about to transition into a new calendar year, and you've seen this very significant multiple compression, I do think where you see high nominal growth, where you see high corporate earnings and a more reasonable multiple, the market setup is still pretty favorable. Chris Hussey: All right, Mark, let's put a bow on it. What's the trade? Mark Wilson: The first one is US-focused. There's been a lot of commentary around the narrowness of the US market performance, and the largest stocks in the index have been the largest spenders. There's been a huge amount of focus on the ROIC and the returns in which these spenders may garner, and I think that the momentum around real AI adoption is beginning to come through, whether it's Muse and other products in the consumer hands, or whether it's some of the enterprise adoption that we're beginning to see, the numbers are clear. And I do think that some of the hyperscaler revenue growth is really lagging by three, four, five, six quarters, the very strong CapEx spend north of 100% that we're seeing, the very, very strong cloud revenue backlog that we're seeing, again, north of 100%. And so, I think as we begin to see some of this ROIC and the real return on spend come through, I absolutely want to be long US mega cap tech. The second one is German fiscal spend beneficiaries. We know how strong the US growth story has been. German manufacturing PMIs are actually outpacing the US right now. Part of that is because as the rest of the world worries about fiscal space, the Germans are able to fiscally expand, and that's driving significant investment across broad industrial complex in Germany. Through this year, you've seen 13 to 14% estimates revisions for EPS, yet those stocks have derated over 20% as well. So right now you're paying low teens multiple for a group of companies that is going to grow earnings in line with the US market over the next 12 and 24 months, so I want to be long that basket of German fiscal spend beneficiaries. Chris Hussey: I love it. US mega cap tech, the harvesters, and the German fiscal beneficiaries. Great. Okay, Mark, last question. What are you watching for next week? Mark Wilson: So, first order I think is going to be CPI next Wednesday. It's going to be all important when we think about what might break this trend of, higher yields. Good news on the inflation front is going to be key. I do think there's a window of opportunity for some news and a break in the Iran conflict given the timing now ahead of the midterms. And then I think all importantly, you mentioned it before, we're going to go into third quarter earnings. We've been in this unique period where really the micro is driving the macro, and I think as we learn more about the state of the AI trade as we go through corporate earnings, that's going to be all important. Chris Hussey: Mark Wilson, you are always a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. title: The Middleweight ADV Bike With BMW GS Comfort And Italian Character - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update BMW’s GS lineup has dominated the adventure bike segment (be it midweight or full-size) for a long time now. But that also means these machines are rather common today. So it’s fair for you–as a potential ADV customer–to want something different but with similar comfort and pizazz as the GS. If that sums up your ADV dilemma right now, we have a solution. It hails from Italy (actually made in Italy, unlike certain Ducatis), has a boxer-like powerhouse, and tops all that with top-drawer comfort for the midweight space. Speaking of today’s midweight space, nearly every bikemaker has entered the party. Some take a really serious approach, like the KTM 890 Adventure R. These are off-road-centric machines first, with a focus on comfort coming as a secondary or tertiary requirement. The Tiger 900 Rally Pro belongs in the same space. Opposite to them are road-biased machines like the Triumph Tiger 850 Sport and Suzuki V-Strom 800 (non-DE). They want to stay on the road as much as possible, although the 19-inch wheel does allow an occasional excursion. All that means there is something for everyone here, whatever your requirements may be. However, things narrow down drastically as soon as you bring Italian character into the mix. You’re technically left with just four or five bikes. Two of these come from Ducati: the fresh DesertX V2 and the Multistrada V2. The former takes the off-road-centric approach, while the latter takes the road-biased approach. So neither has the BMW GS balance we’re looking for. Same goes for the Aprilia Tuareg 660. That leaves us with an off-beat Italian machine from Moto Guzzi, which has the best blend of Italian character and BMW comfort. We’re talking about the V85 TT. This is Moto Guzzi’s answer for the new-age middleweight ADV class, taking on motorcycles from all over the world. Its arch-rival, though, seems to be BMW’s F 800 GS. And the TT does a great job at matching it in some regards, while beating it in others. At the same time, its Italian nature means you get that exclusive swagger you’d expect from a premium brand. Not to mention, Moto Guzzi remains lesser-known in the US, so you’ll surely have people striking up conversations at bike meets. Speaking of which, the V85 is offered in three trims. The Strada serves as the stripped-back base variant, mainly focused toward road riding first evident from the alloy wheels. Then, we have the TT that brings spoke wheels and a couple of other extras for a more ADV-like experience. Last but not least is the touring-ready Travel version. This builds on the TT by throwing in a larger windscreen, hard panniers, heated grips, and a special livery. Out of these, the TT is the most complete, which is why we’re focusing on that here. The V85 TT sells for $12,790. That positions it right in the heat of the midweight ADV segment, above smaller bikes like the Yamaha Tenere 700 and Suzuki V-Strom 800DE, but below more premium bikes like the KTM 890 Super Adventure R and BMW F 900 GS. More importantly, it sits $1,795 more expensive than the base F 800 GS. That isn’t a nice place to be since underrated bikes usually need to undercut direct rivals to stand out in the segment. You should know that the V85’s case gets better once you dive into the details. On that note, the most unique aspect here is arguably the engine. You get a transversal air-cooled 853cc V-twin powerhouse, setting it apart from the sea of parallel-twin rivals. So the cylinders protrude outward from the chassis for a distinct aesthetic. As for output, you get 80 horsepower and 61 pound-feet, with the latter at just 5,100 RPM. That is lower than nearly all of its midweight rivals. You also get variable valve timing for an even better spread of power. All that juice reaches the wheel via a six-speed transmission and final shaft drive. The latter means no worry of chain cleaning every 300 miles. Coming to the chassis, Moto Guzzi has made sure the V85 ticks the essential boxes. A steel trellis chassis is present as the centerpiece, housed on 41 mm USD forks and a monoshock. The shock is laterally mounted instead of in a central position like rivals. While we don’t know the advantage of this, we do know there is 6.7 inches of travel and adjustability at both ends. You even get a remote preload adjuster at the rear–a rarity in this price bracket. Rounding things off are the wheels and brakes. A set of 19/17-inch cross-spoke wheels come standard, featuring dual 320 mm front discs with Brembo monobloc four-piston calipers and a 260 mm rear disc with a two-piston caliper. Overall, the package seems enough for gliding over most stuff you’ll encounter in the real world or on occasional trails. While at it, you’ll appreciate the likable dimensions. The saddle height is 32.6 inches, while the weight is 507 pounds. Considering you get one of the largest fuel tanks (six gallons) in the midweight segment, the weight is impressively low. However, Moto Guzzi hasn’t shed light on the wheelbase, ground clearance, or rake. No Italian bikemaker holds back on tech in 2026, and Moto Guzzi isn’t different. A six-axis IMU and ride-by-wire work in tandem to allow cornering ABS, traction control, ride modes, and cruise control. You access these via a TFT instrument cluster–identical to some Aprilias–that shows a variety of information and has smartphone connectivity for tracking phone info on the fly. Lastly, nitty-gritty bits like LED lights, an adjustable windscreen, an aluminum skid plate, and handguards boost the attention to detail. We want to hear from you. title: Why US Consumers Are Downbeat Despite a Healthy Economy - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Cost-of-living pressures are weighing on US households. However, the downbeat sentiment about the economy among Americans is so widespread that it suggests something else may also be at work, explains Joseph Briggs, who leads the Global Economics team within Goldman Sachs Research. He says the reason may be a broad decline in trust in US institutions. Data show a significant gap between consumer surveys and the sentiment levels that economic models would predict. This suggests that current sentiment survey readings “probably won’t be a very useful tool for economic analysis,” Briggs says. Joseph Briggs: Americans feel worse about the economy than the numbers suggest they should. The question is why? If we look at the consumer sentiment level we’d expect given the fundamentals – a healthy labor market, solid consumer spending, GDP growth – and then the actual average sentiment level, there’s quite a gap. Some of the reasons are intuitive. Cost-of-living pressures, where are most acutely felt by lower-income households, are a main one. But what's striking is that since 2019, just about every group has become more negative on the economy. Whether you look at wealth, income, age, political party, or even social media use, sentiment is down. Americans have become more downbeat overall surveys show. And that in turn is increasingly correlated in declining confidence in institutions. Over the last ten years, almost all of them have seen a drop from science to education, to medicine. So, the final question we ask is what weights more on Americans’ happiness: their level of financial satisfaction or their lack of confidence in institutions? And our analysis shows it’s much more a fundamental, downbeat view on institutions and the state of the world. So as long as consumer sentiment doesn’t really reflect sentiment about the economy, well, it probably won’t be a very useful tool for economic analysis.
